scoring.subdimension_score: Each question measures one subdimension. The chosen option is the subdimension score, a whole number from 0 to 5.
scoring.dont_know: 'I don't know' gives a score of 0 and sets the flag 'insufficient_evidence', as in the chatbot.
scoring.aggregation: Dimension and overall scores, rounding and the report follow the same rules as the chatbot (Sections 2.4 and 2.5).

items.question: How do employees find the data they need for their work?

options.text: There is no way to find data, and nobody has seen this as a problem.
Everyone searches or asks around on their own; it takes a lot of effort and often fails.
Within teams, people know whom to ask or keep their own lists, but this depends on specific people.
There is a documented overview for the whole organization, such as a data catalog, so finding data doesn't depend on specific people.
The overview is maintained by someone responsible and checked regularly for gaps and outdated entries.
The overview is improved continuously based on how people use it and their feedback, supported by automated tools.
I don't know

items.question: Who is responsible for your organization's key datasets?

options.text: No one, and responsibility for data isn't something the organization thinks about.
No one clearly; someone steps in only when a problem occurs.
Within teams it is generally known who looks after which data, but it isn't written down and differs between teams.
Each key dataset has a formally assigned owner, recorded according to one standard for the whole organization.
Ownership is reviewed regularly, and datasets without an owner or owners who have left are found and fixed.
Ownership is improved continuously and built into processes, for example every new dataset gets an owner when it is created.
I don't know

items.question: What is the quality of your data when someone wants to use it for analysis or AI?

options.text: Data quality isn't managed; the data can't be used without being rebuilt.
Individuals fix problems when they notice them; the data needs a lot of manual cleaning every time.
Some teams have their own checks, but quality differs between teams and combining data needs a lot of cleaning.
Documented quality rules apply across the organization, and the data can be used with limited preparation.
Quality is measured against defined thresholds, rules are enforced in the systems, and deviations are corrected.
Measurement results are used to improve the rules continuously, recurring problems are fixed at their source, and monitoring is largely automated.
I don't know

items.question: How do people in your organization approach AI, in their attitude and in their daily work?

options.text: AI isn't used or discussed, and employees have no access to AI tools.
A few individuals try AI tools on their own without guidance; most lack knowledge or confidence.
Some teams use AI regularly and encourage experimenting, while others are skeptical or uninvolved.
The organization supports AI across departments with shared guidelines, and employees are invited to propose ideas.
AI adoption and attitudes are tracked, for example through usage data or surveys, and low adoption is addressed.
Experimenting with AI is part of everyday work, and lessons from successes and failures are shared and used to improve.
I don't know

items.question: Who in your organization has the skills to develop or implement AI?

options.text: No one inside or outside the organization, and the need hasn't been recognized.
Only a few self-taught individuals; AI isn't part of anyone's role.
Some teams have AI specialists or work with external experts, mostly without involving business experts.
AI roles are defined across the organization, and AI work combines technical, business and subject-matter expertise.
AI skills and capacity are assessed regularly, and gaps are closed through hiring, training or partners.
The organization continuously improves how it attracts, develops and keeps AI talent, with career paths for AI roles.
I don't know

items.question: How do employees learn to work with AI?

options.text: There is no AI learning, and the need hasn't been considered.
Employees learn on their own, without training, guidance or sharing.
Occasional workshops or knowledge sharing happen in some teams, but they aren't organized systematically.
A structured AI training programme with practical guidance is available to all employees.
Participation and the effect of training are tracked, and gaps are corrected.
Training is improved continuously based on feedback and new AI developments, and learning is part of daily work.
I don't know

items.question: Has your organization defined what it wants to achieve with AI?

options.text: No, and leadership isn't interested in defining it.
No; individuals have ideas, but nothing is defined.
Some leaders or departments have their own goals for AI, but there is no shared ambition.
A documented AI ambition or strategy for the whole organization states the role AI should play and is communicated to everyone.
The ambition is reviewed regularly, at least once a year, against progress and changes such as new regulation.
The ambition is refined continuously based on results and new developments and actively shapes the long-term direction.
I don't know

items.question: How is AI connected to your organization's business goals?

options.text: It isn't; AI is not considered, or only as a technical topic.
AI is a technical experiment; any objectives are vague, such as "become AI-driven".
Some leaders connect AI to goals in their own area, but without measurable targets.
AI objectives are measurable business targets linked to the strategy, with an executive sponsor and a budget.
Leadership reviews progress against the targets regularly, and missed targets are addressed.
AI objectives are refined continuously and built into strategic planning and decisions.
I don't know

items.question: How does your organization decide which AI ideas to pursue?

options.text: It doesn't; no one has considered where AI could bring value.
Ideas start ad hoc from individual interest or available tools, without any assessment.
Teams choose and fund their own AI projects, each judging them in their own way.
An organization-wide process assesses ideas against criteria such as business value and feasibility, and a designated body decides.
The results of AI projects are measured against their expected value, and weak projects are adjusted or stopped.
The selection process is improved continuously based on past results, and new opportunities are searched for systematically.
I don't know

items.question: How well do your organization's systems support the use of AI?

options.text: Systems are outdated or isolated and can't support AI, and this hasn't been considered.
There are only basic services such as email and file storage; AI is used only through public tools, and data is moved by hand.
Some teams have the systems and tools they need for AI, but systems differ and are mostly not connected.
A common technical environment for the whole organization provides approved AI services, and key systems are connected.
The environment is monitored for availability, performance, usage and costs, and problems are resolved.
The environment is improved continuously, with automated deployment and scaling of AI.
I don't know

items.question: How does your organization obtain AI tools and solutions?

options.text: It hasn't obtained any and hasn't considered how it would.
Individuals choose tools themselves, often free versions, without approval.
Teams buy or build their own solutions, without coordination.
A common approach evaluates tools and vendors against defined criteria, and approved tools and contracts are managed centrally.
Vendors, costs and licence use are monitored, and problems are addressed.
The approach is improved continuously, and build-or-buy decisions are reassessed as needs change.
I don't know

items.question: How does your organization keep its use of AI secure and able to grow?

options.text: There are no controls; anyone may share sensitive data with any AI tool.
A few people are careful on their own, but there are no rules, and AI stays in individual experiments.
Some teams have controls and test their AI, but inconsistently, and pilots rarely spread beyond the team.
Organization-wide rules control which tools may access which data, AI is tested before use, and there is a standard way to roll out pilots.
AI systems in use are monitored and audited regularly, and incidents are detected and addressed.
Controls are improved continuously based on audits and new threats, and monitoring is largely automated.
I don't know
